title: Looks for calls to [Stdin::read_line] to read a line from the standard input into a string, then later attempting to use that string for an operation that will never work for strings with a trailing newline character in it (e.g. parsing into a i32).
summary: The operation will always fail at runtime no matter what the user enters, thus making it a useless operation. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.

title: This lint catches reads into a zero-length Vec.
summary: Especially in the case of a call to with_capacity, this lint warns that read gets the number of bytes from the Vec’s length, not its capacity. Reading zero bytes is almost certainly not the intended behavior. Clippy puts this lint in the nursery group, at the level allow.

title: Looks for calls to RwLock::write where the lock is only used for reading.
summary: The write portion of RwLock is exclusive, meaning that no other thread can access the lock while this writer is active. Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for format trait implementations (e.g.
summary: Display) with a recursive call to itself which uses self as a parameter. This is typically done indirectly with the write! macro or with to_string(). This will lead to infinite recursion and a stack overflow. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.

title: Checks for usage of redundant allocations anywhere in the code.
summary: Expressions such as Rc<&T>, Rc<Rc<T>>, Rc<Arc<T>>, Rc<Box<T>>, Arc<&T>, Arc<Rc<T>>, Arc<Arc<T>>, Arc<Box<T>>, Box<&T>, Box<Rc<T>>, Box<Arc<T>>, Box<Box<T>>, add an unnecessary level of indirection. Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for usage of as_str() on a String chained with a method available on the String itself.
summary: The as_str() conversion is pointless and can be removed for simplicity and cleanliness. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for async block that only returns await on a future.
summary: It is simpler and more efficient to use the future directly. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for [all @ ..] patterns.
summary: In all cases, all works fine and can often make code simpler, as you possibly won’t need to convert from say a Vec to a slice by dereferencing. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for a redundant clone() (and its relatives) which clones an owned value that is going to be dropped without further use.
summary: It is not always possible for the compiler to eliminate useless allocations and deallocations generated by redundant clone()s. Clippy puts this lint in the nursery group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for closures which just call another function where the function can be called directly. unsafe functions, calls where types get adjusted or where the callee is marked #[track_caller] are ignored.
summary: Needlessly creating a closure adds code for no benefit and gives the optimizer more work. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Detects closures called in the same expression where they are defined.
summary: It is unnecessarily adding to the expression’s complexity. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for closures which only invoke a method on the closure argument and can be replaced by referencing the method directly.
summary: It’s unnecessary to create the closure. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for ineffective double comparisons against constants.
summary: Only one of the comparisons has any effect on the result, the programmer probably intended to flip one of the comparison operators, or compare a different value entirely. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.

title: Checks for else blocks that can be removed without changing semantics.
summary: The else block adds unnecessary indentation and verbosity. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for feature names with prefix use-, with- or suffix -support
summary: These prefixes and suffixes have no significant meaning. Clippy puts this lint in the cargo group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for fields in struct literals where shorthands could be used.
summary: If the field and variable names are the same, the field name is redundant. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for unnecessary guards in match expressions.
summary: It’s more complex and much less readable. Making it part of the pattern can improve exhaustiveness checking as well. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for calls to Iterator::cloned where the original value could be used instead.
summary: It is not always possible for the compiler to eliminate useless allocations and deallocations generated by redundant clone()s. Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for redundant redefinitions of local bindings.
summary: Redundant redefinitions of local bindings do not change behavior other than variable’s lifetimes and are likely to be unintended. Clippy puts this lint in the suspicious group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for patterns in the form name @ _.
summary: It’s almost always more readable to just use direct bindings. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Lint for redundant pattern matching over Result, Option, std::task::Poll, std::net::IpAddr or bools
summary: It’s more concise and clear to just use the proper utility function or using the condition directly Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for items declared pub(crate) that are not crate visible because they are inside a private module.
summary: Writing pub(crate) is misleading when it’s redundant due to the parent module’s visibility. Clippy puts this lint in the nursery group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for redundant slicing expressions which use the full range, and do not change the type.
summary: It unnecessarily adds complexity to the expression. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for constants and statics with an explicit 'static lifetime.
summary: Adding 'static to every reference can create very complicated types. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for test functions (functions annotated with #[test]) that are prefixed with test_ which is redundant.
summary: This is redundant because test functions are already annotated with #[test]. Moreover, it clutters the output of cargo test since test functions are expanded as module::tests::test_use_case in the output. Without the redundant prefix, the output becomes module::tests::use_case, which is more readable. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Warns about needless / redundant type annotations.
summary: Code without type annotations is shorter and in most cases more idiomatic and easier to modify. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for casts of references to pointer using as and suggests std::ptr::from_ref and std::ptr::from_mut instead.
summary: Using as casts may result in silently changing mutability or type. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for ref bindings which create a reference to a reference.
summary: The address-of operator at the use site is clearer about the need for a reference. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Warns when a function signature uses &Option<T> instead of Option<&T>.
summary: More flexibility, better memory optimization, and more idiomatic Rust code. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for usage of &Option<&T>.
summary: Since & is Copy, it’s useless to have a reference on Option<&T>. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for usages of the ref keyword.
summary: The ref keyword can be confusing for people unfamiliar with it, and often it is more concise to use & instead. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for regex compilation inside a loop with a literal.
summary: Compiling a regex is a much more expensive operation than using one, and a compiled regex can be used multiple times. This is documented as an antipattern on the regex documentation Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Nothing.
summary: This lint has been deprecated Clippy puts this lint in the deprecated group, at the level none.

title: Lints when the name of function parameters from trait impl is different than its default implementation.
summary: Using the default name for parameters of a trait method is more consistent. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for usage of .repeat(1) and suggest the following method for each types.
summary: For example, String.repeat(1) is equivalent to .clone(). If cloning the string is the intention behind this, clone() should be used. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Looks for patterns such as vec![Vec::with_capacity(x); n] or iter::repeat(Vec::with_capacity(x)).
summary: These constructs work by cloning the element, but cloning a Vec<_> does not respect the old vector’s capacity and effectively discards it. Clippy puts this lint in the suspicious group, at the level warn.

title: Detects assignments of Default::default() or Box::new(value) to a place of type Box<T>.
summary: This incurs an extra heap allocation compared to assigning the boxed storage. Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Nothing.
summary: This lint has been deprecated Clippy puts this lint in the deprecated group, at the level none.

title: Checks for items with #[repr(packed)]-attribute without ABI qualification
summary: Without qualification, repr(packed) implies repr(Rust). The Rust-ABI is inherently unstable. While this is fine as long as the type is accessed correctly within Rust-code, most uses of #[repr(packed)] involve FFI and/or data structures specified by network-protocols or other external specifications. In such situations, the unstable Rust-ABI implied in #[repr(packed)] may lead to future bugs should the Rust-ABI change. Clippy puts this lint in the suspicious group, at the level warn.

title: Informs the user about a more concise way to create a vector with a known capacity.
summary: The Vec::with_capacity constructor is less complex. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for unnecessary ‘..’ pattern binding on struct when all fields are explicitly matched.
summary: Correctness and readability. It’s like having a wildcard pattern after matching all enum variants explicitly. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Disallow the use of rest patterns for accessible fields
summary: It might lead to unhandled fields when the struct changes. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for iterators of Results using .filter(Result::is_ok).map(Result::unwrap) that may be replaced with a .flatten() call.
summary: Result implements IntoIterator<Item = T>. This means that Result can be flattened automatically without suspicious-looking unwrap calls. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for functions that return Result with an unusually large Err-variant.
summary: A Result is at least as large as the Err-variant. While we expect that variant to be seldom used, the compiler needs to reserve and move that much memory every single time. Furthermore, errors are often simply passed up the call-stack, making use of the ?-operator and its type-conversion mechanics. If the Err-variant further up the call-stack stores the Err-variant in question (as library code often does), it itself needs to be at least as large, propagating the problem. Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for usage of _.map_or(None, Some).
summary: Readability, this can be written more concisely as _.ok(). Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for usage of result.map(f) where f is a function or closure that returns the unit type ().
summary: Readability, this can be written more clearly with an if let statement Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for public functions that return a Result with an Err type of ().
summary: It suggests using a custom type that implements std::error::Error. Unit does not implement Error and carries no further information about what went wrong. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Detect functions that end with Option::and_then or Result::and_then, and suggest using the ? operator instead.
summary: The and_then method is used to chain a computation that returns an Option or a Result. This can be replaced with the ? operator, which is more concise and idiomatic. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: This lint warns when a method returning Self doesn’t have the #[must_use] attribute.
summary: Methods returning Self often create new values, having the #[must_use] attribute prevents users from “forgetting” to use the newly created value. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for range expressions x..y where both x and y are constant and x is greater to y.
summary: Also triggers if x is equal to y when they are conditions to a for loop. Empty ranges yield no values so iterating them is a no-op. Moreover, trying to use a reversed range to index a slice will panic at run-time. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.
